rows.q: What does Katz mean by imperative exchange?
rows.a:
"Imperative exchange" is Katz's name for the most basic way humans relate to the center once the originary scene has given way to ritual. The center commands; the community obeys; and in obeying, the community issues a request back. Each side gives an imperative and expects one to be honored in return.

## Where it comes from

On the originary scene the central object "tells" the group to stand back, to defer appropriation. Once that scene is repeated as ritual, the center keeps commanding, but it is also addressed. Katz puts it this way: the central locus "now receives imperatives along with issuing them, and is therefore increasingly defined by this dialogue with the community, what I have been calling an 'imperative exchange'" ([The Discourse of the Center](/post/the-discourse-of-the-center#p-3)).

His clearest example is sacrifice. The worshipper bringing a goat to the altar "is following an order issued by the deity to offer up some of the fruits provided, ultimately, by that deity; while, in exchange, the sacrifice represents a request... that the deity continue providing these benefits (more goats)" ([Beyond "Post-Sacrificial"](/post/beyond-post-sacrificial#p-1)). Ritual in general works the same way: "the participant fulfills some command of the center while making a request of the center. It is an asymmetrical imperative exchange" ([Languaging Practices](/post/languaging-practices#p-2)). It is asymmetrical because the center gave first and gives more.

Katz also says when the exchange starts up: it "results from ostensive failure, and aims at restoring an ostensive relation to the center" ([Ostensive-Imperative Generativity](/post/ostensive-imperative-generativity-and-scenic-design-practices#p-3)). When the shared object is no longer simply present to be pointed at, we start commanding and petitioning in order to get it back. The meal was granted, and we ask for the next one.

## Why it drives so much else

**When the exchange fails, thinking begins.** Sometimes the gods do not deliver. Myth comes in here, to explain the failure: the ritual must have been done wrong, or the god has other purposes. More generally: "Thinking begins with the failure of some imperative exchange—I did this, but reality didn't supply that." The declarative sentence is "the conversion of a failed imperative exchange into a constraint" ([Cognition as Originary Memory](/post/cognition-as-originary-memory#p-25)). The declarative is a lesson drawn from a deal that didn't hold.

**It escalates.** The logic of exchange keeps raising the price. The more the center is understood as having given us, the more we owe, up to "your first born" ([The Sovereign Remembering of Names](/post/the-sovereign-remembering-of-names#p-8)). This is how Katz links imperative exchange to human sacrifice and the divine emperors.

**Monotheism breaks it, and not by asking less.** The God whose name is a declarative sentence ("I AM THAT I AM", a reading Katz takes from Gans) cannot be bargained with. "There is no more commensurability and therefore no more exchange" ([Cognition as Originary Memory](/post/cognition-as-originary-memory#p-24)). God demands "all of you, all the time." This is what Katz means by the post-sacrificial order. Prayer then refines into the purest form of the exchange, almost its dissolution: "help me to know how to donate to you" ([Mimesis, the Center and Auto-Immunology](/post/mimesis-center-auto-immunology#p-40)). You no longer bargain for goods. You ask for clearer instructions.

**But it never goes away.** "Imperative exchange cannot be eliminated—it is embedded in our habits... if I do this, reality will supply that" ([Cognition as Originary Memory](/post/cognition-as-originary-memory#p-25)). The modern citizen who thinks "I played by the rules, so the institution owes me" is still living inside it, and resentment is what that feels like when the exchange seems broken.

## In the recent essays

Katz now makes the concept central to his account of technology and finance. Technology is "the perfection of the imperative": you build systems so that your commands are fulfilled reliably. He calls the imperative exchange, together with the ostensive-imperative-ostensive loop, a kind of "chora," a space where desire emerges at the threshold of articulation ([Perfecting the Imperative and Imperative Exchange](/post/perfecting-the-imperative-and-imperative-exchange-originary-fintech#p-1)). Using our devices takes the shape "petition meeting command" ([Media, Technology and Originary Grammar](/post/media-technology-and-originary-grammar#p-19)): tell me how to do what you are telling me to do.

## Try it on something

Take any institution you deal with, such as an employer, a university or a government office. What does it command of you, and what do you take yourself to be requesting in return by obeying? Then ask what happens to your relation to it when you stop haggling over what you are owed and start asking how better to fulfill its commands.

**Read next:** [Beyond "Post-Sacrificial"](/post/beyond-post-sacrificial) for the move from imperative exchange to what Katz calls "interrogative imperativity," and [Cognition as Originary Memory](/post/cognition-as-originary-memory) for how failed exchange gives birth to the declarative and to thinking itself.

rows.a:
Short answer: no. But Katz doesn't treat that as a dismissal, and the reasons why are a good way into the whole field.

**Why it can look like one**

Center Study rests on the originary hypothesis: language, the human and the sacred begin together, in a single event. A group of proto-humans converges on a desired object. One gesture turns from grabbing into pointing (an "aborted gesture of appropriation"), the others repeat it, and violence is deferred. The object at the center becomes, in Katz's phrase, the "Name-of-God." That is an origin story with a sacred center, and Katz admits the resemblance openly:

"I do have to acknowledge that GA is odd in being very similar to a religion and at the same time the exact opposite of one. It is an 'origin story,' and it can feel like one is being asked to 'believe in' something." ([The Originary Hypothesis in Itself](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-4))

He goes further. Taking the hypothesis on board may require "something like a conversion experience... you'd have to be able to abandon and revise all 'priors'" ([p-6](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-6)).

**Why it isn't one**

First, it asks for a different stance than belief. Katz says belief is something "I don't 'believe' in." The hypothesis asks instead for "a willingness to live or think in a kind of 'suspense'" ([p-4](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-4)). A hypothesis is held open to scrutiny and revision. A faith commitment is held fast.

Second, its relation to religion is explanatory, from one level down. It claims to account for why there are faiths at all:

"in a way it is the antithesis of faith and religion by disclosing the originary possibility of all faiths and religions." ([Originary Hypothesis as Mobius Strip](/post/originary-hypothesis-as-mobius-strip#p-1))

The consequence is uncomfortable. If you take the hypothesis literally, you can only see your own tradition "as an approximation of a configuration you consider prior and irreducible to that tradition." Believers do work within the field, but there is a real tension there.

Third, it doesn't side with secular debunking either. It isn't Enlightenment critique, because "the implication of the originary hypothesis is that the faiths are truer than philosophy, and it's not even close" ([p-2](/post/originary-hypothesis-as-mobius-strip#p-2)). Katz's summary of the odd position is "a perfectly materialist refutation of materialism, the one true faith masquerading as subversive heresy." So it is closest to the faiths and furthest from them at the same time, and it can't be absorbed by philosophy.

**A further twist**

Katz is suspicious of the word "religion" itself. It isn't minimal enough, since there may be "no single phenomenon called 'religion'" across cultures ([Inscription](/post/inscription#p-2)). He prefers more basic terms such as commemoration: the community's repeated practices of remembering, which let it say "this is the same" ([p-3](/post/inscription#p-3)). On this view, religions, rituals, and even liberalism with its saints and taboos ([Desecration](/post/desecration#p-1)) are all forms of commemorating the center. Center Study is the inquiry into that, which is why Katz can say that, pressed on what he believes, his answer would be "language."

**Where to read next**

- [The Originary Hypothesis in Itself](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself) is Katz's most candid account of why people resist the hypothesis, the "faith" problem among the reasons.
- [Originary Hypothesis as Mobius Strip](/post/originary-hypothesis-as-mobius-strip) works out the "closest and furthest" paradox and what it demands of anyone who takes it seriously.

A question to try: think of a practice you would never call religious, such as a national holiday, a sports ritual, or a workplace habit. Ask what it commemorates, and what violence or breakdown it keeps at bay.

rows.q: What is thirdness in Katz's recent essays?
rows.a:
In the recent essays (roughly 2023–2025), "Thirdness" is the name of a *project*: an imagined company, partly a journal, partly an arbitration firm and partly a prediction market. It puts into practice Katz's argument that the juridical, the settling of disputes by an impartial third party, is the medium through which the imperative of the center now reaches us. The word also has an older philosophical sense in his writing, and the recent project grows out of it, so I'll take both in turn.

## Where the name comes from

Katz explains it directly. Thirdness is "a reference to Washington's third man as well as Peirce's concept of generality and significance created through agreement" ([Thirdness](/post/thirdness#p-22)).

The "third man" comes from George Washington's will, which Katz quotes. Washington provided that any dispute among his heirs be decided by "three impartial and intelligent men, known for their probity and good understanding," two chosen by the disputants and the third chosen by those two, who would rule "unfettered by law, or legal constructions" ([Thirdness](/post/thirdness#p-8)). What appeals to Katz is that this is judgment in its pure form: not legal technicality, but "a 'sense' of the juridical" that he thinks has been eroding for decades ([Thirdness](/post/thirdness#p-9)).

The Peircean side goes back further. In an early GABlog post Katz describes thirdness as "the recipient and normalization of the interplay of firstness and secondness, founding and institutionalization, but it is also the position of the witness or spectator" ([The Single Source of Moral and Intellectual Innovation](/post/the-single-source-of-moral-and-intellectual-innovation-gablog#p-11)). In a 2015 post he says civilization itself "depends upon deferral to the judgment of the 'third person'" and on everyone cultivating that person's dispositions ([Flouting Civilization](/post/flouting-civilization#p-11)). The recent Thirdness turns that stance, the ability to step back and see a conflict as a case to be judged, into an institution.

## The core idea: every event as a case

The starting premise is strong: "nothing 'happens' that could not be framed as including potential claimants before some tribunal" ([Thirdness](/post/thirdness#p-1)). Katz places the juridical between ritual (the originary distribution, or *nomos*) and the disciplinary (organized inquiry), and treats it as the "irreducibly human" layer ([Thirdness](/post/thirdness#p-4)). To understand an event, such as a war, is to "sort out claims and counter-claims the respective sides do and might make against each other and the kind of tribunal that might sit in judgment" ([Thirdness](/post/thirdness#p-4)).

At first this was to be a journal publishing such case framings. If its judgments proved good enough, it would grow into an arbitration firm that disputants in good faith would choose. Those "interested in honing grudges for the sake of institutional blackmail would avoid the firm like the plague" ([Thirdness](/post/thirdness#p-6), [p-7](/post/thirdness#p-7)).

## Why a prediction market

Next Katz adds betting. Ordinarily we can only bet on events with official closure, such as games and elections, and that depends on trusting whoever certifies the outcome ([Thirdness](/post/thirdness#p-11)). Thirdness would make any event bettable by constituting it as a case with a judgment to come. You would be betting less on the event itself than on the judgment rendered ([Thirdness](/post/thirdness#p-14)).

The key design choice is that cases are framed to sit as close to 50/50 as possible. The house simply takes its cut like a bookie, and the uncertainty lies in the deliberation itself, not in some hidden lean of the judges ([Thirdness and the Same Sentence](/post/thirdness-and-the-same-sentence#p-1), [p-2](/post/thirdness-and-the-same-sentence#p-2)). In practice this pushes toward marginal or idiosyncratic cases. Instead of asking whether a defendant is guilty, Thirdness might ask whether a media outlet will correct a specific legal claim made in its coverage ([Thirdness and the Same Sentence](/post/thirdness-and-the-same-sentence#p-4)). The point is pedagogical. Bettors learn to think the way the judges think, and anyone who consistently outguesses the team should be recruited onto it ([Modeling Thirdness](/post/modeling-thirdness#p-13)).

## The harder part: judgment as data exchange

What Katz calls "difficult and new" about Thirdness is that settlements would take the form of *data exchange* instead of punishment or damages: "each party donating and/or receiving data from the center in lieu of such things as punishment or damages" ([Modeling Thirdness](/post/modeling-thirdness#p-2)). A defamation case, for instance, might settle through a guarantee of rapid retractions or a revision of the algorithms that determine how a story circulates, not through money. The settlement's language could itself be adopted into a team's public documents and function as "capital" ([Thirdness and the Same Sentence](/post/thirdness-and-the-same-sentence#p-23), [p-25](/post/thirdness-and-the-same-sentence#p-25)). In this sense Thirdness is "idiom mining": each judgment generates new, precise ways of speaking that can circulate as currency, which Katz elsewhere calls *learncoin* ([Mining Idioms in Thirdness](/post/mining-idioms-in-thirdness#p-12), [p-13](/post/mining-idioms-in-thirdness#p-13); [Learncoin](/post/learncoin#p-10)).

All this pursues a paradox Katz takes seriously: "the perfection of the juridical would be its abolition." If judgment became thorough and predictable enough, disputes would be anticipated and deferred before they arose. The bet, finally, is on which ruling makes it more likely "that Thirdness will be abolished as it is taken up in all everyday practices" ([If… Then](/post/if-then-the-idiom-of-data-exchange-substack#p-23)).

## An application

Katz's own example is a brief clash between protesters and a police officer, framed as a suit in both directions. The protesters are asked to give a theory of justice and the state that would justify their actions. The officer is asked what resource from his training could have handled the situation better. The question to be judged becomes whether the officer embodied "a representation of the center, that someone in that situation would have been obliged to respect and obey" ([If… Then](/post/if-then-the-idiom-of-data-exchange-substack#p-19), [p-20](/post/if-then-the-idiom-of-data-exchange-substack#p-20)). Notice the move. A culture-war flashpoint, usually played out as a vendetta in the media, is converted into a case whose outcome teaches both sides something about the other's likely future conduct.

## How seriously to take it as a plan

Katz is candid that it is speculative. He leaves it "open source" and admits it may remain a "dissident" model of justice rather than a functioning institution ([Thirdness](/post/thirdness#p-19), [p-25](/post/thirdness#p-25)). He also says it should probably begin as a conventional online journal ([Modeling Thirdness 2](/post/modeling-thirdness-2#p-16)). His Nomos/Class Action proposal is the "far less esoteric" practical cousin ([Nomos/Class Action](/post/nomos-class-action#p-15)).

**Read next:** [Thirdness](/post/thirdness), the founding statement with the Washington passage and the market design, and then [Thirdness and the Same Sentence](/post/thirdness-and-the-same-sentence), where the 50/50 logic becomes a way of thinking and writing as well as a way of betting.

**An exercise:** take a dispute currently in the news and find the version of it that is genuinely 50/50. Not the question of who is guilty, but some narrower question whose answer would actually teach you something.

rows.q: What does Center Study suggest about how to write a good prompt for an AI?
rows.a:
Katz never writes a how-to on prompting, but he comes back to prompts often, and his originary grammar gives a fairly specific account of what a good prompt does. In short: a prompt is an imperative addressed to a kind of center. A good one is built so that what comes back opens the way to the next, better imperative.

## 1. Prompting continues an old practice

Katz is reluctant to treat prompting as a technical novelty. He places it in a line that runs back to ritual:

> "We're trying to draw out imperatives from the center—what should we do, how should we contribute to the center so as to be worthy of and receive its bounty—whether this is done by more rehearsal of a chant and dance or by revising a prompt or search term eliciting information from the center is the aim." ([Nomos and Transfer Translation](/post/nomos-and-transfer-translation#p-20))

"The center" here means whatever gathers shared attention and whose commands we try to hear. Katz increasingly calls the data and algorithms we all contribute to the "central intelligence". Seen this way, prompting is a form of **imperative exchange**, the model Katz takes from prayer: I obey, I ask, I find out from the response how my asking fell short, and I ask again. The ritual analogy is a practical point. When the result disappoints, the fault usually lies in how you asked, and the fix is to revise the asking, not to repeat it louder.

## 2. Measure a prompt by the next prompt it makes possible

Katz, drawing on Brian Roemelle, defines prompt engineering as

> "the designing of search terms that would elicit results from searches into textual databases (i.e., AI) that will most powerfully suggest the design of a new search term." ([Techno-Grammar](/post/techno-grammar#p-1))

So you don't judge a prompt by whether it produces a finished answer. You judge it by whether the answer points you to a sharper question. In the same essay Katz maps this onto the sequence of speech forms from Gans's *The Origin of Language*:

> "the search is conducted by giving the 'AI' … imperatives and asking it questions. The prolongation of the ostensive into the imperative, the imperative into the interrogative and the interrogative into the declarative studied by originary grammar will prove its potency here as well… those imperatives that can make the trek through to the declarative will be 'selected for.'" ([Techno-Grammar](/post/techno-grammar#p-11))

In plain terms, a good prompt has all four layers:

- **Ostensive**: you point to something specific and shared. Paste the passage, name the case, show the object. A prompt without anything pointed at leaves the model to supply the "average" referent.
- **Imperative**: you say what is to be done with it.
- **Interrogative**: you hold the imperative open as a real question, so the model has space to tell you something you don't already know.
- **Declarative**: the answer comes back as statements. Their value lies in the new things they let you point to, which become the ostensive of your next prompt.

## 3. Bland prompts return the average

Katz tested this himself. He asked ChatGPT about AI and creativity and got an encyclopedia entry. His diagnosis:

> "perhaps it's my fault for asking such a bland, predictable question—precisely the kind one would open an encyclopedia to answer." ([Review of Mark Amerika](/post/double-helix-v10-amerika-review#p-8))

Because a language model continues text toward the probable, "the more unpredictable your writing, the more 'interesting' the range of continuations of it you will receive" ([same review](/post/double-helix-v10-amerika-review#p-17)). This is why he predicts we "will learn to prompt ever more surrealistically" ([Brute Force Computation](/post/brute-force-computation-and-the-debt-to-the-center#p-2)). It also connects to his account of the **idiom**. If your prompt is written in commonplaces, you get commonplaces back. If it carries a distinctive idiom, with its own terms, juxtapositions and constraints, the model has to work within that idiom. His proposal to train a model on center study's idioms, "prompting the model to translate contemporary texts of all kinds into a more centered discourse" ([Universal Translation Machine](/post/universal-translation-machine#p-9)), is the same principle at a larger scale.

## 4. Specify whose intention you are extending

Katz describes the best use of LLMs as "the prolongation of intention." For him, the familiar question "what would X do?" can only be answered if you construct the distance between X and now:

> "we'd have to figure out who, exactly, was George Washington (and which texts, of Washington and others, do we draw upon, and how do we weigh them…)" ([Thinking only through Models](/post/thinking-only-through-models#p-16))

For prompting, this means three things. Name the model you are drawing on. Name its sources. Make the gap between its world and yours part of the task, instead of asking it to pretend the gap isn't there.

## 5. The prompter is also being prompted

In his review of Dobrin, Katz notices that once we start "think[ing] in potential 'prompts,'" the AI is no longer a tool we stand outside of: "The system is using us as much as we are using it" ([AI and Writing](/post/writing-pedagogy-katz2#p-11)). The skill that results is "prompting and selecting from among the results of the prompt and then iterating this practice over and over again" ([p-10](/post/writing-pedagogy-katz2#p-10)). A good prompter therefore keeps track of what they kept, what they discarded, and why. Those choices are the real record of your thinking.

## Applying it

Take a student who types: *"Explain mimetic desire."* That is the encyclopedia prompt. A version shaped by Katz's account might read:

> "Here is paragraph 8 of Katz's 'Mimetic' lecture [pasted]. Here is a situation from my workplace [described]. Read the situation through that paragraph. Point out where my own account of it already assumes I am not imitating anyone, and propose one question I should ask next."

This prompt points at specific things (the paragraph and the case). It gives a command. It leaves room for something the student can't see. And it explicitly asks for the next prompt. The answer becomes the material for the following round.

## Reading next

- [Techno-Grammar](/post/techno-grammar): the fullest treatment of prompting as originary grammar.
- [Review of Mark Amerika](/post/double-helix-v10-amerika-review): Katz prompting ChatGPT himself, and his reflections on writing as remixing through the machine.

**Exercise:** take a prompt you used recently and mark which of the four speech forms it contains. Then rewrite it so that it includes the one that was missing, usually the ostensive.

rows.q: What does deferral mean? Explain it like I'm fifteen.
rows.a:
Imagine a group of very early humans, not quite humans yet, standing around a fresh kill. Normally the strongest eats first, then the next strongest, and so on. But this time everyone wants it at once, because each of them sees the others wanting it, and that makes it look even more desirable. They all start moving toward it together. If nothing changes, they will tear each other apart.

Then one of them hesitates. His reaching hand slows down and becomes something like pointing instead of grabbing. The others notice and copy it. For a moment nobody grabs, and everyone is looking at the thing and at each other. Center Study calls this the **originary scene**, and that hesitation is the first **sign**: the beginning of language, of the human, and of the sacred all at once. The thing in the middle becomes the **center**, the place everyone pays attention to instead of fighting over.

That hesitation is **deferral**: putting off the grab, and with it the violence, by turning an action into a sign.

## Why not just say "prevent" or "postpone"?

Katz insists on the word. When you "postpone" something, you have already decided, calmly and from the outside, to do it later. Deferral isn't like that. You are inside the situation and can't see how it ends:

> "Instead of preventing imminent destruction, we have really done no more than make it 'imminently imminent,' and that imminence of imminence gives us a little space within which to work." ([Lecture 3: Deferral of Violence](/post/deferral-of-violence#p-4))

You don't fix the problem forever. You buy a little room, and in that room something new can happen. He also says deferral "posits no endpoint. As long as there is humanity there is deferral" ([Deferral, Debt and the Idiom](/post/deferral-debt-and-the-idiom#p-1)). We never finish doing it.

## Deferral isn't just waiting

You might think it means "always hold back," and that more waiting is always better. Katz answers that directly. Kids made to sit at the dinner table until 7 aren't better people than kids fed at 6. What matters is that the meal is *framed*: everyone at the table, someone says grace, nobody grabs food off another plate ([The Generativity of Deferral](/post/the-generativity-of-deferral#p-6)). Deferral means doing things *through* shared signs and forms instead of just grabbing. And the feeling isn't misery, because "the effect is of a new world opening up" ([The Generativity of Deferral](/post/the-generativity-of-deferral#p-1)). When two friends stop fighting over something, the thing they were fighting over can suddenly become funny.

## It's everywhere around you

Say you nearly bump into someone in a hallway and say "excuse me." Katz uses exactly this example. You are heading off a tiny conflict right now, and you're also repeating every earlier "excuse me," a little *institution* of deferral that politeness is built from ([Tokenizing Deferrality](/post/tokenizing-deferrality#p-10)). Manners, rules in games, courts instead of revenge, waiting your turn to talk: all of these are deferral that has become habit. Katz lists the bigger versions: courts defer the blood feud, and a stable government defers everyone's fight over who gets to be in charge ([Style: Markers and Measurements of Deferral](/post/style-markers-and-measurements-of-deferral#p-5)).

That's why Center Study's short formula is *representation is the deferral of violence*. Every word you use is a distant descendant of that first hesitation over the kill.

## Try this

Next time you're in an argument, look for the moment when someone stops and says something instead of shoving: a joke, a "hold on," a rule ("that's not fair"). That's deferral. Ask yourself what it put off, and what new possibility it opened.

**Read next:**
- [Lecture 3: Deferral of Violence](/post/deferral-of-violence): a short lecture, the clearest full treatment of why "deferral" is the right word.
- [The Generativity of Deferral](/post/the-generativity-of-deferral): answers the obvious objection ("can't you defer too much?") with everyday examples.

rows.q: How would Center Study read a social media pile-on?
rows.a:
Center Study reads a pile-on as a small, fast iteration of the originary scene going wrong. Many people converge on one center, and nothing defers the convergence. Here are the layers, building from that.

## 1. The convergence is mimetic

Katz uses the pile-on as his everyday example of what he calls *violent centralization*, meaning attention converging on someone in a way that tends toward their expulsion:

> "have you ever felt (and given into) the temptation to 'pile on' someone who is being criticized, attacked, or ridiculed? There is no way you would have been thinking of the clever bon mot you are about to add without the mimetic instigation of those who have already dropped a couple." ([Revivalistics](/post/revivalistics#p-1))

The point is that the pile-on doesn't feel mimetic from the inside. Each person experiences their quip or condemnation as their own judgment. But the desire to add one comes from watching others add theirs. That is mimesis in its rivalrous mode: everyone becomes the same, all looking at one figure and all trying to outdo each other in the same gesture.

Katz is careful to add that a theory of scapegoating needs a boundary. "We must be permitted condemnation of wrong actions, sharp and uncompromising critiques... otherwise, how could we even address the problem of scapegoating without engaging in it ourselves?" (same paragraph). So the question isn't whether criticism happened. It is what kind of convergence took place.

## 2. The scene is a vicarious trial

Social media scales this into what Katz calls the Big Scene: a scene with no limits, where everyone is imagined as present and as qualified to judge. His analysis of mass media applies directly. The media, he says,

> "perpetually position us as judges on events involving some purported transgression, commanding us to 'take a position' and add our little quantum of power to whatever target is being displayed on the Big Scene (and Big Screen)." ([Media as Ritual](/post/media-as-ritual#p-1))

And more sharply:

> "All the media does is stage trials and invite the audience to participate vicariously as judges, jurors and, increasingly, enforcers." ([Media as Infrastructural Translation](/post/media-as-infrastructural-translation#p-13))

A pile-on is that trial with every procedure removed: no standing, no evidence rules, no judge, no sentence proportioned to the offense. Katz's notion of the *juridical* is useful here. For him, law is a historical achievement that caps the vendetta by moving conflicts into adjudication. A pile-on is a vendetta that has borrowed the vocabulary of justice. It is the kind of thing the juridical exists to defer.

## 3. What the pile-on is really aimed at: the center

This is where Katz goes beyond a generic Girardian reading. In Girard (I am drawing on him here, not on the archive), the scapegoat is typically marginal. Katz argues that violent centralization is ultimately directed at the center, at authority. It is driven by the suspicion that someone has usurped it:

> "violent centralizations... always, at whatever scale, seek to find and punish a hidden power imagined to lie behind the scenes of the official power." ([The Center, Speaking](/post/anthropomorphics-the-center-speaking#p-13))

So the target of a pile-on is almost always cast as someone who got away with something: a celebrity, an institution, a "privileged" person, a public figure who was too powerful to be held to account. The crowd acts as an informal tribunal because it believes the formal ones have failed. That is resentment in Katz's strict sense, resentment toward a center that hasn't distributed justly. The crowd then deploys that resentment against whoever is standing in for the center at the moment.

The scene also generates the opposite posture. The target, or the target's defenders, can take on the role Katz calls the *exemplary victim*, "the one who is denounced or ignored by all but whom history will vindicate" ([Lecture 4: The Center](/post/the-center#p-17)). Pile-on and counter-pile-on mirror each other, with each side claiming the persecuted position. That is why social media fights so rarely end. Each round produces material for the next.

## 4. Why the medium amplifies it

Katz takes up the popular "digital orality" thesis, the idea that social media returns us to the polarized, tribal intensity of oral culture. He grants its plausibility but calls it incomplete:

> "Social media retribalizes us, on this account. But this leaves the Stack out of account... It's a consumerist approach to the question." ([The Sentence as Metric](/post/the-sentence-as-metric#p-1))

For Center Study, then, the pile-on isn't simply something that "the crowd" does. It runs on designed infrastructure: algorithms, amplification, and what Katz elsewhere calls scenic design. Who gets put at the center is partly a product of who controls the machinery. That is why he insists on asking, of any media event, "who wants us to know this, why in this way" (see the archive's discussion in [The Scene is the Same](/post/the-scene-is-the-same)).

## 5. What Center Study recommends doing

Katz's answer is neither neutral nor a call to abstain. It has three parts.

**Don't counter-pile.** Turning the accusation back on the accusers ("you're the real bigot") just takes part in the same scene. Katz explicitly warns against this reflex in the context of accusations like "racist" ([Nomos/Class Action](/post/nomos-class-action#p-17)).

**Redesign the scene.** Social media, he says, is better used "to design social interactions or 'interfaces' that foreground dangerous markings along with ways of deferring their danger" ([Design and the Attentional Economy](/post/design-and-the-attentional-economy#p-14)). This means pointing out how a target has been *marked*, and offering another way of seeing them, before the convergence completes.

**Put yourself on the scene too.** In his most recent work, Katz argues that anyone who centers someone else becomes centerable in turn. The responsible utterance therefore does both at once: "let all your utterances (samples) be as close to 50% directing attention to the other and 50% drawing attention to yourself as possible" ([Idiom and the differend](/post/idiom-and-the-differend#p-16)). If you do criticize, make your own investment visible as you do it. That move turns a pile-on into something closer to a scene of shared attention.

His more institutional proposal is to move these fights back into actual juridical channels, through real defamation and fraud cases. He imagines that "wars on social media would be transformed from exchanges of insults and spite into evidence collection missions" ([Nomos/Class Action](/post/nomos-class-action#p-10)).

## Applying it

Take an ordinary case: a clip of someone behaving badly in a store goes viral. A Center Study reading would ask a series of questions. Who was put at the center, and what marked them (class, politics, appearance)? What failed authority is the crowd standing in for: the store, the police, "the system"? What lets people join in without cost (likes, the safety of numbers)? What would a gesture of deferral look like here? Possibly asking what actually happened before the clip began. And what does your own impulse to comment reveal about your position on the scene?

## Where to read next

- [Media as Infrastructural Translation](/post/media-as-infrastructural-translation) is the fullest account of media as vicarious trial, and of Katz's alternative.
- [Idiom and the differend](/post/idiom-and-the-differend) develops "originary satire" and the 50/50 ethic of speaking about others.

To try it yourself: take the last pile-on you saw and write down what the crowd believed the formal authority had *failed* to do. Then ask whether the pile-on did that thing or only performed it.

rows.q: Quote the passage from Katz's essay "The Algorithmic Center" where he defines machine deferral.
rows.a:
I can't give you that quotation. No essay called "The Algorithmic Center" is among the texts I've been shown, and nothing I have defines "machine deferral." I won't reconstruct a passage that may not exist. If you have a link or a copy, share it and we can read it together.

The idea behind your question does come up in the archive, though, and Katz's position runs almost opposite to what "machine deferral" suggests. For him, deferral is what machines lack:

> "All that differentiates us fundamentally from the machines, and for the better, is deferral—the deferral of appropriation, which is the source of all human creation." ([Brute Force Computation and the Debt to the Center](/post/brute-force-computation-and-the-debt-to-the-center#p-23))

Deferral here is the originary gesture: the hand reaching for the shared object at the center turns into a sign and stops short. Mimesis, envy and resentment, Katz says in the same paragraph, "will still distinguish us from the machines, but in such a way as to make us inferior by most measures." Only deferral marks a difference that counts in our favor.

Katz doesn't treat the algorithm as an enemy to be resisted. He sees it as the form the center takes now. In "Sampling on the Data Exchange" he imagines the program telling you what to read, then revising your sentence, then writing the essay. He asks why anyone would keep running it if no one were participating in the inquiry, and concludes:

> "What only humans can contribute to the center, then, is forms of linguistic presence." ([Sampling on the Data Exchange](/post/sampling-on-the-data-exchange#p-22))

"Linguistic presence" means keeping a scene of shared reference going, so that we can keep saying "this is the same." The machine can calculate on the scene. Sustaining the scene is the human contribution.

The closest Katz comes to machinery that *carries* deferral is in [Deferral as Media](/post/deferral-as-media#p-11). There, well-designed algorithms help us "think probabilistically, to project probabilities further and further into the future," which he calls "really the essence of deferral." The deferring is still done by people. The algorithm extends how far ahead they can defer. In *Anthropomorphics* he puts our choice under algorithmic conditions as becoming "either predictable and unreliable, or unpredictable and reliable." The second means extracting and improving the imperative embedded in the machine's categories ([Anthropomorphics](/post/anthropomorphics-book#p-344)).

**To read next:**
- [Sampling on the Data Exchange](/post/sampling-on-the-data-exchange) is his fullest treatment of writing alongside the algorithm. It explains why machine translation and text generation work by "chunks," and what remains for the human.
- [Brute Force Computation and the Debt to the Center](/post/brute-force-computation-and-the-debt-to-the-center) ties AI to originary debt and gratitude toward the center.

A question to try: if deferral can't be handed off to the machine, what would it mean to *train* a machine on our acts of deferral rather than on our appropriations?

rows.q: What does Katz say about climate change?
rows.a:
Climate change is not a topic Katz takes up directly. It comes up in passing, always as an example for something else he is working out. Those passing remarks are consistent, though, and they show how Center Study handles an issue like this: it neither argues the science nor takes a side in the culture war. It asks what the issue does to power, responsibility and the center.

## 1. Treat it as a question of power matched to responsibility

His most useful remark is in "Be an Interface Between Power and the User":

> "The climate changers claim they want to save the planet—what kind of power, social and technological, would have to be composed so as to meet that responsibility? And once it was composed, of course, it might find it has other things to do than pump carbon out of the atmosphere." ([Be an Interface Between Power and the User](/post/be-an-interface-between-power-and-the-user#p-14))

This is the "central imaginary" applied to climate. Whenever someone says "we should" do something at planetary scale, they are imagining an authority able to do it. Katz asks you to picture that authority concretely, and then to notice that an authority with that much capacity would not simply carry out the demand that called for it. It would govern. So "save the planet" is really a claim about what kind of sovereignty we want, made without saying so.

## 2. Redesign the habitat instead of reducing carbon

Reviewing Benjamin Bratton's *The Stack*, Katz suggests that what really draws people to ecology is "the pretext it provides for design projects that would match the scope of the supposed problem," and then turns it around:

> "if, rather than obsessing over trying to minimize (and even shrink) the amount of carbon in the environment, we were to say, 'well, why don't we just accept that all the things the climate changers say is going to happen—melting polar caps, flooded coastlines, super-storms and the rest—will happen and redesign our human habitat in response,' we'd have an 'absolutist' or 'autocratic' project precisely parallel to Bratton's in scope, ambition, and disregard for present political pieties." ([The Stack, the City](/post/the-stack-the-city#p-2))

The phrase "supposed problem" shows his skepticism, but he does not argue the science. He moves the question from guilt and reduction to scenic design: building the stage humans will act on. This fits a theme that runs through his work, that technology is the design of scenes.

## 3. Watch the climate issue as a mechanism for silencing

In "The Offspring of the Progenitor of Lies," climate appears in his list of truths or reasonable claims that cannot be voiced. Politicians, he notes, are looking into suing oil companies "for disagreeing with the ruling doctrine on the 'climate change' formerly know as global warming" ([The Offspring of the Progenitor of Lies](/post/the-offspring-of-the-progenitor-of-lies#p-7)). Here climate is a case of victimary politics turning certain claims into thought crimes.

## 4. Elsewhere he sets it aside

Reviewing Daniel Ross, he puts the question in brackets ("whatever one's views of… the question of climate change") so he can get to what interests him: a global economy run by megacorporations "beholden to no sovereign power" ([Mimesis, the Center and Auto-Immunology](/post/mimesis-center-auto-immunology#p-32)).

## A note on the Gans texts

Two passages in the archive are by Gans, not Katz. "Ending White Guilt" is Gans's Chronicle 337, which uses global warming as a "Rorschach test." In Gans's reading, the victimary thinker *wants* human beings to be to blame, because taking all the blame quietly assumes our own omnipotence ([Ending White Guilt](/post/ending-white-guilt#p-2), [p-4](/post/ending-white-guilt#p-4)). The afterword to *The Origin of Language* calls climate change "apocalyptic." Katz builds on Gans's account of the victimary, but these are Gans's words.

## Where to go next

- [The Stack, the City](/post/the-stack-the-city) shows the habitat-design argument in context and how Katz thinks about planetary computation and sovereignty.
- [Be an Interface Between Power and the User](/post/be-an-interface-between-power-and-the-user) gives the power/responsibility method, which you can apply to any large policy demand.

As an exercise, take a current climate proposal and write out the chain of command it would need to work as advertised. Then ask what that authority would actually do once it existed.

rows.q: Katz famously wrote that "resentment is the engine of history." Which essay is that from?
rows.a:
I can't find that line anywhere in what I've been shown, and I'd be wary of the attribution. None of the texts in front of me contain the sentence "resentment is the engine of history," and I won't name an essay I can't point to. If you saw it quoted somewhere, it may be a paraphrase, or it may be closer to Eric Gans than to Katz. Gans has written extensively on resentment in his *Chronicles of Love & Resentment*.

The attribution also cuts against something Katz says explicitly. He argues that resentment does not scale up into a cause of large historical movements:

> "Does resentment simply not scale up, and is therefore to be discarded in political thinking? I don't think referring to the decisions of big players—corporate leaders, finance chiefs, intelligence agency heads, etc.—as driven by resentments will be very productive" ([Muffled Transmission from the Center](/post/muffled-transmission-from-the-center-substack#p-17))

He goes further: "Governance involves the transcendence of resentment, on the part of ruled and ruler alike, and mimetic theory and GA must both deny this possibility, even while the originary hypothesis presupposes its possibility" ([same essay](/post/muffled-transmission-from-the-center-substack#p-18)). Explaining the actions of rulers by their resentment, he adds, describes "dysfunction, not 'human nature.'" Part of his break with Gans was a complaint that Generative Anthropology's handling of resentment stays at the scale of "a 19th century French novel." He calls that tendency the "Big Scenic Imaginary": treating whole populations as if they were individuals resenting one another on a single small scene.

Here is where the archive comes closest to your phrase:

- **Gans, as quoted by Katz:** "history only gives us models for putting it off, for spreading it thin enough to let some light pass through its opacity" (Chronicle 144, quoted in [Resentment](/post/resentment#p-2)). In this view history is the *deferral* of resentment, not something resentment drives. In that essay Katz then asks why Gans never considers the most obvious way resentment gets contained, which is the juridical, the courtroom.
- **Katz on Gans's list:** Gans names Eve, Achilles, the Exodus and the crucifixion as products of resentment. Katz takes this up in [Resentment, Good and Bad](/post/resentment-good-and-bad-some-reflections-on-eric-gans-s-latest-chronicle-the-tri#p-7). If you want something that sounds like "resentment moves history," that list is the nearest thing, and it is Gans's.
- **Katz's own small twist:** "maybe the resentment towards theories of history is the source of theories of history" ([A Little Social Theory](/post/a-little-social-theory#p-20)).

Katz's positive position is captured better by his own coined phrase: "donate your resentment to the center." He defines resentment institutionally rather than as a feeling. In his words, it is "your fulfilling of an imperative, having the reciprocal imperative you issue go unfulfilled, while not letting that reciprocal imperative lapse" ([Resentment](/post/resentment#p-19)).

**To read next:** start with [Resentment](/post/resentment), which is his fullest engagement with Gans on this exact question. Then read [The Tokenization of Resentment](/post/the-tokenization-of-resentment), where he works out what "donating" resentment to the center actually involves.

If you can tell me where you came across the quotation, I can help you work out whether it is a misattributed Gans line or a compression of one of these passages.

rows.q: What does Center Study say about dreams and the unconscious?
rows.a:
Honest answer first: Katz has no sustained treatment of dreams, and only a handful of passages on the unconscious. But those passages fit together, and they show how Center Study would approach the subject. In short, it would not treat the unconscious as a hidden room inside the individual. It would treat it as one of the names we give to whatever acts on us from beyond conscious decision, which Center Study calls the center.

**1. "The unconscious" is a borrowed center**

The key move is in "The Disciplines, the Imperative of the Center, the Generative Thought Experiment." On the originary scene the central object is the first agent; humans get their agency by borrowing it from the center. Katz says this has never stopped:

> "the modes of central being we now borrow from are now figures called 'society,' 'ideology,' 'the unconscious,' 'the media,' and so on." ([The Disciplines, the Imperative of the Center…](/post/the-disciplines-the-imperative-of-the-center-the-generative-thought-experiment#p-2))

So "the unconscious" is a figure we put at the center to account for the part of our thinking and acting we did not choose. Katz says plainly that this residue is real: "there are dimensions of our thinking and doing that lie beyond conscious decision" ([#p-9](/post/the-disciplines-the-imperative-of-the-center-the-generative-thought-experiment#p-9)). Then he relativizes the explanations, psychoanalytic ones included:

> "saying that the trauma caused by my parents, or unjust social structures, or unconscious desires, etc., are not all that different from saying I was tempted by the devil." ([#p-9](/post/the-disciplines-the-imperative-of-the-center-the-generative-thought-experiment#p-9))

He calls these explanations "black boxes, sites of proxy wars for power," adding that "To be master of the 'unconscious' is to be master of much more" ([#p-10](/post/the-disciplines-the-imperative-of-the-center-the-generative-thought-experiment#p-10)). What he puts in their place is the idiom of **imperatives from the center**. When you seem driven by something you did not choose, you are hearing competing commands, picked up from many earlier scenes, that have "no expiration date," and you resolve them by tracing them back to a higher authority ([#p-12–14](/post/the-disciplines-the-imperative-of-the-center-the-generative-thought-experiment#p-12)). What psychoanalysis calls unconscious content becomes, here, unexamined imperatives.

The same demotion appears in "Selfy," which describes Freud's "Copernican turn": consciousness "was on the margin, not at the center" ([Selfy](/post/selfy#p-2)). Katz accepts that consciousness sits on the margin. He disagrees with Freud about what occupies the center.

**2. Why Katz still respects Freud**

In an early piece Katz gives psychoanalysis credit that he denies neurobiology:

> "at least Freud put desire, violence and deferral at the center of his psychology, and saw the central problem of humanity as relations between humans…" ([Violent Imaginaries](/post/violent-imaginaries#p-7))

This essay offers the nearest thing in the archive to an "originary theory of the unconscious." Katz argues that the all-consuming melee the first sign averted probably never could have happened literally; it was a **violent imaginary**, the scene completed in imagination ([#p-3–5](/post/violent-imaginaries#p-3)). Every sign, he says, is backed by such an imaginary, which can be read negatively from the sign. This imaginary is the unconscious in Center Study's terms: the imagined catastrophe that our signs are shaped to ward off. Like Freud, Katz holds that it cannot be made fully conscious, because representing it only "shift[s] the terms" ([#p-9](/post/violent-imaginaries#p-9)). What can be done is to make it "the imaginary of the scene of representation itself," a scene of dialogue or discipline built to work through it ([#p-10](/post/violent-imaginaries#p-10)). On this reading the analytic session is one scene in a long series that leads back to the originary scene ([#p-8](/post/violent-imaginaries#p-8)).

**3. Dreams specifically**

Dreams themselves come up only in passing.

- In "Successful Succession," dreams mark the limit of control: "You can't control your dreams, but you can prevent your dreams from interfering with your management of your household." Drawing that line belongs to "the maintenance of subjectivity," and Katz adds: "who knows, maybe such maintenance acts back upon your dreams" ([Successful Succession](/post/successful-succession#p-5)).
- "Inscripto-punctualism" points the other way: "The more you know about your 'unconscious' the more you produce both greater consciousness and a more generative unconscious" ([#p-12](/post/inscripto-punctualism#p-12)). Attending to the unconscious does not drain it. It makes it more productive.
- A 2014 GABlog post, which comes before Center Study proper, calls dreams "creative and unpredictable" and doubts that brain activity could ever be decoded into conscious content ([Thought Experiment](/post/thought-experiment#p-8)). Read it as background. It is not doctrine.

**4. Applying it**

Suppose you keep dreaming of being publicly accused. A Freudian looks for a repressed wish. A Center Study reading asks other questions. Which scene does this come from? Whose imperative is still sounding, without an expiration date? What violent imaginary (the convergence of everyone on you, which is the scapegoat position) is the dream completing, the way imagination completes a lawn beyond a wall? The useful work is not decoding the dream. It is building a scene, such as talking it through or writing, in which that imaginary can be shared and a sign of deferral found for it.

Katz never says this directly; it is an extrapolation from the passages above. Dream interpretation as a practice is Freud's, and the archive says nothing about method.

**Read next**

- [Violent Imaginaries](/post/violent-imaginaries) is the fullest bridge between psychoanalysis and the originary hypothesis.
- [The Disciplines, the Imperative of the Center, the Generative Thought Experiment](/post/the-disciplines-the-imperative-of-the-center-the-generative-thought-experiment) shows the "competing imperatives" method that replaces appeals to the unconscious.

A question to work on: if "the unconscious" is a borrowed center, which earlier center did it replace? Katz's comparison with "tempted by the devil" suggests an answer.
